docs.title: W1: Role-based redesign, payments, and CI/CD debugging
Starting point
docs.text: CreditSetu already had a working scoring pipeline (XGBoost + SHAP, cold-start bootstrap for SHG vs. independent borrowers) and a single combined frontend where every role could see every other role's data -- no login gate except an optional borrower self-service view. This week's work replaced that with proper role separation and added a live repayment flow.

docs.title: Problem: everyone could see everyone else's data
docs.text:
There was no access control. A borrower, a lender, and an SHG all hit the same open API and the same combined UI.

Fix: four separate login-gated roles -- Borrower, Lender, SHG, Admin -- each with its own dashboard and its own bearer-token session table, modelled on the existing borrower "My Score" auth pattern (PBKDF2 hashing, opaque tokens, no JWT). Critically, authorization is enforced server-side on every endpoint (401 for no/bad token, 403 for wrong-role or out-of-scope access), not just hidden in the UI -- verified this by hitting the API directly with a borrower's token trying to fetch another borrower's record and confirming a 403.

Lenders and SHGs didn't have credentials at all before this, so I added username/password_hash columns to both tables and a migration script that seeds demo credentials (slug-of-name + password123, same pattern as borrowers) without touching any of the existing seeded business data.

docs.title: Feature: lender reputation
docs.text: The product ask was "lenders should get some benefit for offering better interest rates -- check if anything like this exists in the real world." Landed on RBI's priority-sector-lending / co-lending incentive structure as the real-world analogue, and implemented a reputation score computed from each lender's own base_interest_rate relative to the platform average, plus their actual marketplace activity -- entirely derived from existing schema fields, no new fabricated data.

docs.title: Feature: targeted loan requests + a live repayment flow
docs.text:
Two gaps reported after the first role-based pass went live:

  1. A borrower's loan request always broadcast to every eligible lender; there was no way to target one specific lender from the suggested list. Added an optional target_lender_id on the request, plus a retarget endpoint so a declined targeted request isn't a dead end.
  2. There was no way to actually repay a loan -- the dashboard showed loan status but repayment history only ever came from the offline synthetic data generator, never from a live borrower action.

The second one needed a real design decision: what does "amount due this cycle" mean for a loan that might have been disbursed seconds ago, with no due-date/collections engine in the app at all? Solved it by deriving the cycle number from the count of existing repayment events on that loan rather than elapsed calendar time, so a brand-new loan is payable immediately -- this is what makes the feature usable by a live demo user, not just replayable against backdated data.

Added a wallet_balance per borrower (seeded as a multiple of their existing monthly_income, not an arbitrary number) and a payment endpoint that: re-fetches the balance inside the same transaction right before deducting (a minimal guard against a real race condition, since this codebase has no row-locking anywhere else either), blocks payment of any loan if the wallet can't cover the borrower's total dues this cycle (not just the one loan clicked -- this was an explicit product requirement, not my own interpretation), and recomputes the credit score in the same commit so the impact is visible immediately.

Verified end to end with a real account: requested a loan, approved it from a lender login, paid it through the new flow, and watched the score move from 596 (Medium risk) to 886 (Very Low risk) after enough on-time history accumulated -- entirely through the live API, no manual database edits.

docs.title: Bug found: risk labels read backwards
docs.text: "Very Low" risk was being shown bare under a borrower's own score -- technically correct (very low risk of default) but reads as if the score is bad. Relabelled to the same Excellent/Good/Fair/Poor/Very Poor language real credit bureaus use, as a pure display-layer mapping in the shared score-badge component (no backend/schema change).

docs.title: Bug found: link approve/reject was silently broken
docs.text: While checking the SHG and Admin dashboards, found that the "Approve Partnership" / "Reject Partnership" buttons on the lender dashboard referenced l.link_id, but the actual API field is id. Every click was calling the decide endpoint with undefined -- this wasn't just a React key-prop console warning (which is what first drew my attention to it), it meant lenders could never actually approve or reject an SHG link through the UI. Fixed all three occurrences plus the matching one on the admin links table, and confirmed live that approving a real pending link now correctly moves it to Approved.

docs.title: CI/CD: the docs site wasn't actually deploying
docs.text: Added docs/summary.md so mkdocs-literate-nav had something to build a sidebar from (it never existed, inherited gap from the upstream template). That alone didn't fix it, though -- the deployed site was still rendering via GitHub's default Jekyll README fallback, not the repo's own mkdocs GitHub Actions workflow. Root cause: GitHub disables workflow files by default on a fork that already contained them at fork time, so the mkdocs workflow had never run once, ever, despite being correctly written and correctly triggering on push. Fixed by enabling workflows on the fork (Actions tab banner, not the general permissions settings), then pointing GitHub Pages' source at the gh-pages branch the workflow produces instead of master. Also found and fixed a same-story 404 on every page for javascript/arithmatex.js, referenced in mkdocs.yml for KaTeX math rendering but never created -- added it as a documented no-op stub since nothing in the docs actually uses math notation yet.

docs.title: What I'd flag for next week
docs.text:
• Prototype Stage report template is still marked TBA on the course site -- nothing to fill in there until it's released.
  • Score-history "improvement over time" features (home page stories, district trend stats) are real but sparse right now, since the scoring pipeline has only been run a handful of times -- they'll fill in naturally as more scoring runs happen, not something to force with fake history.

docs.title: W2: Prototype Stage report, UML diagrams, and toolchain setup
Verified the SHG and Admin dashboards, found another real bug
docs.text: Checked both role dashboards live. SHG dashboard was clean. Admin dashboard worked but surfaced a real defect while I was in there: the "Approve Partnership" / "Reject Partnership" buttons on both the Lender and Admin dashboards referenced l.link_id, but the actual API field is id. Every click silently called the decide endpoint with undefined -- lenders could never actually approve or reject an SHG link through the UI, despite the button looking functional. Fixed all occurrences and confirmed live: a real pending link now correctly moves to Approved.

docs.title: Drafted the Prototype Stage report
docs.text: No official course template exists yet for this report (still marked TBA on the course site), so I built one from an approved reference format -- matched its heading structure (Abstract/Keywords, Introduction, Related Work, Proposed Methodology with an Algorithm subsection, Results and Analysis, Conclusion, References) and adapted the content to CreditSetu instead of copying its subject matter. Added a Feasibility Report section (Technical/Operational/Economic/Schedule) and three new appendix sections for UML diagrams, per the explicit instructions given for this report. Every number and claim in the report is one we actually measured or verified this session or the previous one -- nothing padded.

docs.title: Allocated agents for the three UML diagrams
docs.text:
Ran three parallel agents, each reading the real codebase before drawing anything, to produce PlantUML source for: - Use case diagram -- 4 actors, ~40 use cases, plus 6 fully written use-case scenarios (preconditions/main flow/alternate flows/ postconditions) grounded in the actual routers. - Class diagram -- from the real SQLAlchemy models, all 16+ tables including the role-session and payments-feature additions. - Activity diagram -- the real request -> approval -> repayment -> rescoring flow with Borrower/System/Lender swimlanes, including the actual race-condition guard and the aggregate insufficient-funds gate.

The use-case agent independently caught the same class of bug I'd just fixed: the borrower dashboard's "Recompute my score" button called POST /api/individuals/{id}/recompute-score, which is admin-only by design (documented in our own spec). Every click would have 401'd. Removed the button, replaced it with accurate copy explaining that the score updates automatically after each repayment.

docs.title: Rendering and compiling: three tool installs
docs.text: None of this could be verified without local tooling, so: - Installed poppler (pdftoppm) so I could actually read PDF content as images instead of taking a file's existence on faith. - Installed PlantUML (needs Java, already present) and rendered all three diagrams to PNG locally -- caught that the use-case diagram is visually dense (expected, given 4 actors x ~40 use cases) but confirmed all three render without syntax errors. - Embedded the rendered PNGs into the report as real \includegraphics figures.

docs.title: Debugging why Overleaf wasn't showing the diagrams
docs.text: A manual ZIP upload to Overleaf lost the figures/ folder's relative position to main.tex, so every \includegraphics fell back to LaTeX's "file not found" placeholder (a bordered box with the literal filename printed inside -- not an error, easy to miss why it's happening). Diagnosed this by walking through exactly what Overleaf's upload flow preserves vs. flattens, rather than assuming the diagrams themselves were broken.

docs.title: Installed MiKTeX locally and compiled for real
docs.text:
Rather than keep guessing at fixes for Overleaf's upload behaviour, I installed a full LaTeX distribution (MiKTeX) locally -- first attempt was interrupted by a GUI confirmation dialog mid-install (scoop's wrapper didn't handle it), so I re-downloaded the installer directly from the CTAN mirror and ran it with the correct --unattended --auto-install=yes flags. Compiled main.tex with pdflatex (two passes, for cross-references), then verified the result by rendering the output PDF back to page images myself and visually confirming all three diagrams are genuinely embedded and legible -- not just trusting a "compile succeeded" message. Pushed the working PDF to the repo.

This means the project no longer depends on Overleaf working correctly to get a compiled report -- there's now a working local LaTeX toolchain that can rebuild either report from source at any time.

docs.title: W3: Testing the repay flow end to end, two data bugs, and fixing a noisy score
Starting point
docs.text: The payments feature from W1 (wallet balance, live repayment, score recompute in the same commit) had only been checked once, by hand. Before building on it I ran it end to end properly: through the API with error cases, then through the real UI in a browser, against a backed-up copy of the database so the test payments could be undone afterwards.

docs.title: What the end-to-end test confirmed
docs.text: Via the API (borrower 424): a payment moved the wallet by exactly the EMI, cut the loan's outstanding balance, advanced the cycle (EMI #6 -> #7), and stored a new score row. The error paths all behaved: paying someone else's loan -> 403, viewing another borrower's due summary -> 403, nonexistent loan -> 404, wallet too small -> 400 with the balance and the amount due, no token -> 401. In the UI I logged in, went through the demo payment-gateway sign-in, paid a loan, and checked the wallet, the "Paid ... Late" banner, the new score and the database rows all agreed. No console errors apart from the app's normal logged-out /auth/me 401s.

docs.title: Bug found: a loan with nothing owed was still payable
docs.text:
Loan 619 had a 0.00 outstanding balance but was still Active, and the Repay page offered to charge a full EMI for it. Root cause was in the synthetic data generator, not the payment code: it tracks the balance as principal only (principal - paid_total) while every EMI includes interest, so loans hit zero before their last cycle -- and the generator only closed a loan if it reached zero and its final cycle. 64 loans were affected.

Fix: the generator now closes any loan whose balance reaches zero; a one-off idempotent migration (migrate_close_paid_loans.py) closed the 64 existing ones (second run closed 0); and the payment service skips loans with nothing owed and closes a loan when its balance reaches zero.

docs.title: Bug found: a missed cycle stayed "due" forever
docs.text:
The cycle number was derived by counting only On_Time and Late events, so a Missed or Partial event never moved the pointer. Loan 620's Missed 2026-08-21 row sat next to a computed due date of 2026-05-23, and the cycle that had already been recorded as missed could never be cleared. There were 2,071 Missed and 1,583 Partial events in the data.

Fix: every recorded event now resolves its cycle, so the pointer advances past a Missed or Partial cycle. Loan 620 went from EMI #14 to

docs.title: 18. I updated the formula in API_CONTRACT_PAYMENTS.md to match. One
docs.text:
consequence worth knowing: Active loans whose events already cover their whole tenure, but which still carry a balance (196 of them), no longer show as payable -- a missed cycle is treated as written off, not as arrears to catch up. Making arrears payable would be a separate design decision.

Re-ran the whole flow in the UI afterwards: Household (619) gone from the list, Small business at EMI #18, payment took the wallet down by exactly the EMI, database rows consistent.

docs.title: Investigation: the score went down (and up) after late payments
docs.text:
While testing I noticed a borrower's score moved in ways that didn't match the payment: 852 -> 848 after one late payment, then 848 -> 860 after another, including one 179 days overdue.

I tested it counterfactually without touching the database -- recompute the score for the same borrower with one extra On_Time, Late or Missed event added. For borrower 424, an On_Time payment, a Late one at 5 days and a Late one at 179 days all gave the same -5. Across 271 SHG-linked borrowers the average direction was right (On_Time +4.9, Late -3.1, Missed -31), but per borrower it was unreliable: 19% saw an On_Time payment lower their score, 17-21% saw Late score above On_Time.

Two causes:

  1. No monotonicity. The XGBoost model was unconstrained and trained on only 474 people, so it fit noise: raising late_rate from 0.18 to 0.25 raised one borrower's score (847 -> 864), and 200 average days late scored above 100.
  2. n_repayment_events as a feature. It measures how long someone's history is, not how well they repay, and every payment of any kind bumps it by one -- one extra event moved a score by 5 points and the feature swung it by up to 87 points over a narrow range.

I also realised part of the 852 -> 842 I'd seen was my own loan-closing migration changing n_closed_loans for 64 borrowers, leaving stored scores stale until the next scoring run.

docs.title: Fix: monotone constraints, drop the length feature, retrain, rescore
docs.text:
Before changing the real model I compared variants in a scratch script using 5-fold cross-validation, because a single 95-person holdout is too small to trust: unconstrained 0.915 AUC, monotone 0.913, monotone without n_repayment_events 0.916 -- accuracy unchanged, behaviour much better.

Applied it: n_repayment_events removed from the model's feature list (still computed for the cold-start blend and anomaly check), monotone constraints added in train_scoring_model.py (more on-time/savings/ attendance/peer repayment can only lower default risk; more late/partial/ missed or days late can only raise it), model retrained, then score_all re-scored all 1,079 borrowers (history is kept -- new rows are appended).

Before After On_Time payment lowers score 19% 0% Late scores higher than On_Time 17-21% 5% Missed scores better than On_Time not measured 0% (36% ties)

docs.title: Final run: everything together
docs.text:
After all four fixes (loan closing, missed cycles, scoring, lender names) were in, I ran the whole repay flow once more from a backed-up database and restored it afterwards. Borrower 424 started at wallet Rs. 14,272.50.

Through the API: the due summary now listed two loans (Household 619 gone), each with a lender name ("Rural Trust NBFC") and the Small business loan at EMI #18 of 24. Paying it moved the wallet to 13,198.09 -- exactly the EMI -- recorded a Late payment (59 days) and lowered the score 858 -> 849, the direction the new model is supposed to move. Every error case still behaved: paying the already-closed loan 619 -> 400, someone else's loan or due summary -> 403, unknown loan -> 404, wallet too small (borrower 1: 774.71 against 1,293.50 due) -> 400 insufficient_funds, no token -> 401.

Through the real UI: logged in as the borrower, opened Repay, signed into the mock gateway, and the page already reflected the API payment (wallet 13,198.09, Small business at EMI #19). Each row now read "Rural Trust NBFC · Purpose" instead of a blank lender. Paying the Agriculture loan showed "Paid Rs. 2,052.66 -- Late", moved the wallet to 11,145.43 (13,198.09 - 2,052.66) and advanced the cycle EMI #6 -> #7. The database matched: two new Late repayment events (59 and 46 days), reduced loan balances, and score rows noted "Recomputed after live repayment". The server log had no 500s -- the only 401/403s were the app's own pre-login session check and my deliberate wrong-owner / no-token tests -- and the database was restored to its starting state (wallet 14,272.50, 16,993 events) at the end.

Scope of that run: one borrower through the UI (plus one more for the insufficient-funds case), not the whole population.

docs.title: Feature: a guided demo inside the app
docs.text:
To present the system without clicking through four logins by hand, I added an in-app guided demo, modelled on the one in my RL autoscaler project. A "Guided demo" button in the navigation (and on the home page) opens a choice of five tours:

Tour Steps Changes data? End-to-end: loan request to repayment (all four roles) 16 Yes: 1 request, 1 loan, 1 payment Borrower 15 Yes: 1 request (then withdrawn), 1 payment Lender 11 No Self-help group 7 No Bank / admin 10 No

The tour drives the real app rather than a recording: it logs in through the real login form, opens pages, types and clicks, highlights the element each step is about, and explains it in a panel at the bottom. The panel has a step counter, a list to jump to any step, Previous / Next, auto-play that moves on when the narration ends, spoken narration through the browser's speech engine (with a voice picker that prefers a natural male English voice), Hide text and Close.

Three design decisions mattered:

  • Demo accounts are discovered, not hard-coded. Phone numbers change every time the data is reseeded, so the tour signs in as the admin behind the scenes and picks an SHG member who has a payable EMI and an eligible lender, plus that lender and the member's SHG, and checks those logins work before using them.
  • Data-changing steps run once per tour. Going back with Previous shows the earlier result again but never repeats a request, approval or payment. Each step marks itself done just before its irreversible click, so even a step that fails afterwards is not repeated. I checked this against the database: jumping back to the payment step left exactly one repayment.
  • Navigation is locked while a step is still working, so skipping ahead cannot interrupt a payment halfway.

I ran every tour step by step in the browser: all 16 + 15 + 11 + 7 + 10 steps passed, auto-play advanced on its own, and narration started when the voice was turned on. The database was restored afterwards.

docs.title: Bug found by the guided demo: a paid-off loan vanished
docs.text: The borrower tour's payment step timed out on its first run, even though the payment had gone through. The payment closed the loan (its balance reached zero), the Repay page reloaded the due list, the closed loan dropped out of it, and its row disappeared together with the "Paid" confirmation. A real borrower paying off a loan would have seen it simply vanish. The page now keeps each paid row on screen with its result and says when the loan is fully repaid and closed.

docs.title: What I'd flag
docs.text:
• About 68% of borrowers see no change at all from a single extra On_Time payment: one event is too small to cross a split in a model trained on ~475 people. That is a data-size limit, not a bug.
  • The remaining Late-above-On_Time cases (5%) are mostly legitimate: a late payment of fewer days than the borrower's average lowers their avg_days_late.
  • Holdout AUC on the single 95-person split dropped 0.910 -> 0.900; the cross-validated numbers show no real difference.
  • Fixed afterwards: lender_name came back null for every loan in the due-summary, because the generator deliberately seeded all ~1,650 historical loans with no lender ("pre-marketplace history"), so the repay page couldn't say who was being repaid. Backfilled by migrate_loan_lenders.py following the marketplace's own rules (an Approved-linked lender for SHG members, an independents-serving one for independents; deterministic by loan id, idempotent, live-flow loans untouched, 0 rule violations checked in SQL) and the generator now does the same. 38 loans whose SHG has no approved lender stay unattributed and show "Lender not recorded" instead of a blank.
  • The mock payment gateway's abc/123 credentials are hard-coded in the frontend -- fine for a demo, not for anything shown outside one.

docs.title: W5: The borrower's own view — history, explanation, and tips
Starting point
docs.text: The borrower dashboard has one job the other three do not: it is the only screen a non-technical person is meant to read on their own. A lender can be trained; a borrower gets one look. So this week was spent on the three panels that have to carry meaning without explanation — score history, the SHAP breakdown, and the improvement tips.

docs.title: Bug: the score history ran backwards
docs.text:
The history chart plotted the score rows in the order the API returned them, which is newest first. The x-axis therefore ran from today back to the first score, so a borrower whose score had steadily improved saw a line sloping down.

Nobody reads an axis before they read a slope. The one fact the chart exists to convey — "this is going up" — was inverted for every borrower on the platform.

Fix: order ascending by calculated_date before plotting. Trivial change, and a reminder that a chart's default is whatever order the query happened to produce, which is a property of the database, not of the story being told.

docs.title: The explanation panel
docs.text:
The SHAP contributions are stored per score, in score points, and drawn as a waterfall. Two decisions were worth making carefully:

  • Anchor on the population baseline, not the floor. Allocating the contributions as a share of score - 300 makes the explanation almost empty for exactly the borrowers scoring near 300 — the people who most need to know what is wrong. Measuring against the model's own baseline prediction keeps the breakdown meaningful at both ends.
  • Name the features in plain language. avg_days_late is not a phrase anyone uses. The panel shows what the feature means in the borrower's own terms, with the sign and the size of its effect.

docs.title: Improvement tips
docs.text:
The tips are generated from the negative contributions only, capped at five. The constraint I settled on: a tip must describe an action the borrower can take, not a fact about them. "Your SHG's repayment rate is low" is not actionable by one member; "pay your instalments on time — late payments are currently costing you the most points" is.

Some features cannot produce a tip at all for this reason — the SHG peer rate and the district are about where someone is, not what they do — so they are excluded from the tip generator even though they move the score.

docs.title: Because
docs.text:
The dual-path design exists to be explainable. If the chart points the wrong way and the breakdown collapses to nothing for the lowest scores, the explanation is decoration — and a decorative explanation is worse than none, because it implies a transparency that is not there.

The test I kept applying: could a borrower read this screen and know what to do differently next month? If not, the panel is not finished.

docs.title: W6: Who decides whether a borrower can pay — the wallet or the loan?
Starting point
docs.text: The repay page had a rule inherited from the first version of the payments feature: a borrower may pay only if the wallet covers the total dues across all their active loans this cycle. Running the demo path repeatedly made me doubt it, so this week was spent deciding what the rule should actually be and changing it.

docs.title: The two candidate rules
docs.text:
Aggregate. Compute every active loan's EMI for this cycle, sum them, and block every payment unless the wallet covers the lot.

Argument for: it stops a borrower clearing the small loan while silently defaulting on the large one, and the system never helps someone into a worse position than they started.

Per loan. Each loan is checked against its own EMI. If the wallet covers that instalment, it can be paid.

Argument for: it matches what the borrower is actually being asked to do. They are paying this loan. A borrower with three loans and enough money for one is better off paying one than paying none, and the aggregate rule makes the second-best outcome impossible.

docs.title: What settled it
docs.text:
The aggregate rule produced a screen that could not be explained to the person reading it. With two loans and enough for the first, the page showed an affordable instalment next to a blocked button, and the reason — "you also owe something else later this cycle" — was nowhere in the borrower's mental model of the action they were taking.

Worse, it makes the system an enforcement mechanism it was never designed to be. Refusing a payment someone can afford, in order to protect them from a position they are already in, is a policy decision. The project has no mandate for it, and no lender asked for it.

Fix: switched the sufficiency check to per-loan. The due summary still shows the total across all active loans, so nothing is hidden — the borrower can see the full picture and decide — but the gate on each payment is that loan's own instalment.

docs.title: Edge cases that came with it
docs.text: Evaluating each loan on its own is also what later exposed two bugs in the loan state: fully repaid loans that were still offered for payment, and Missed cycles that could never be cleared. They were found and fixed in the end-to-end run written up in W3, so the details are there rather than repeated here.

docs.title: Because
docs.text: A rule that protects the user from themselves needs a stronger justification than a rule that does what the user asked. The aggregate check had the better-sounding argument and the worse behaviour: it blocked affordable payments, it could not explain itself on screen, and it quietly assumed an authority over the borrower's choices that the product does not have.

docs.title: W7: Making the project reproducible by someone who is not me
Starting point
docs.text:
Everything in the repository worked on my machine, which is the weakest form of working there is. With the evaluation ahead and a final report to write, the question became: if an examiner clones this at 9 a.m., can they have it running by 9.10, and will they get the same numbers we quote?

The honest answer was no, for three different reasons.

docs.title: What was missing
docs.text:
The run instructions assumed knowledge. The README said how to start the API and the frontend, but not that the database has to be generated first, nor that the model artifacts have to exist before the API can serve a score. Someone following it literally got a running server and empty dashboards.

The migrations were undocumented. Three one-off scripts exist — closing fully-paid loans, attributing seeded loans to lenders, and the auth/payments schema migrations — and nothing told a new reader when to run them or whether running them twice was safe. (They are idempotent, which is exactly the kind of fact that is worthless if it is only in the author's head.)

Order mattered and was unstated. data_gen → train_scoring_model → score_all is not a sequence anyone can guess, and running it in the wrong order fails in ways that look like bugs: scoring with no model, training with no data.

docs.title: Fix
docs.text:
Rewrote code/README.md around the path a stranger actually takes:

  1. install dependencies,
  2. generate the synthetic population (seed fixed at 42, so the numbers in the report are reproducible),
  3. train the scoring model,
  4. score the whole population,
  5. run the API and the frontend,
  6. log in with the demo accounts — listed, per role.

Each one-off migration is listed with what it does, when it is needed, and the fact that re-running it is harmless.

docs.title: The reproducibility point
docs.text:
The seed matters more than it looks. Every figure quoted in the reports — population counts, loan totals, the default rate, holdout accuracy — comes from a dataset generated with seed=42. If the generator changes, those numbers move, and a report that cites them becomes wrong without anyone touching the report.

That has already happened once: the November changes to the generator (closing fully-paid loans, attributing loans to lenders) shifted the loan status breakdown and the default rate from what the Prototype Stage report quotes. Not an error in either document — but the Final Report has to state which dataset its numbers came from, or the two reports simply contradict each other.

docs.title: Because
docs.text:
A project that only runs in the hands of the person who wrote it has not been delivered, it has been demonstrated. The difference shows up at exactly the wrong moment: when someone else, under time pressure, tries to make it work.

Writing the README properly took an afternoon and is the single change most likely to matter to whoever opens this repository next — including us in four weeks, when the details have gone.

docs.title: W8: Writing the Final Report from what the system actually does
Starting point
docs.text:
The Prototype Stage report was written in a hurry in W2 and described a system that was still moving. The Final Report has to describe one that has stopped — and every number in it has to come from a run somebody actually did, not from the previous report.

So the first task was not writing. It was deciding which claims could survive being checked.

docs.title: Re-deriving the figures
docs.text:
Worked through the report's claims one at a time, re-running what each depends on:

  • Population: taken from the demonstration database the system actually runs on, and labelled "at the time of writing". A fresh seed with the current generator gives slightly different counts, because the generator itself changed in November.
  • Loan status breakdown and default rate: these moved since the Prototype Stage report, because the generator now closes fully-paid loans and attributes historical loans to lenders. The Final Report quotes the current dataset and says so, rather than silently carrying the old figures forward.
  • Model performance: re-measured after the monotone retrain rather than reused.
  • The live journey: re-run end to end — request, approval, repayment, rescore — and the report quotes that run.

Anything I could not re-derive came out of the report. That removed two sentences I liked and could not substantiate.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
Built on the TIET template, with the figures carried over from the prototype stage (use case, class, activity, swimlane) and a note in the text wherever the system has changed underneath them since — the 16 features that are now 15, and the wallet rule that is now per loan.

references.bib collects the sources properly instead of the hand-written bibliography the earlier draft used — XGBoost, SHAP, Isolation Forest, k-means, PBKDF2, the UML specification.

docs.title: What the report says that the prototype one did not
docs.text:
The defects. D-01 (all seeded borrowers share one password hash) and D-02 (401 where the specification says 403) are both in the Final Report with their severity and recommended fix, along with the limitations that are design decisions rather than bugs: shared demo passwords, the hard-coded mock gateway login, the fact that score history is short because the batch scorer has only been run a handful of times.

The argument for including them: an examiner who finds a defect we did not mention concludes we did not test. An examiner who finds one we listed, with a fix proposed, concludes we did.

docs.title: Because
docs.text:
The temptation in a final report is to describe the system as designed rather than as built, because the design is tidier and the build has edges. But the edges are the evidence of engineering — the monotone constraint exists because the score misbehaved, the per-loan check exists because the aggregate one blocked affordable payments, the storage listener exists because a logged-out tab kept rendering.

A report that hides those reads as a specification. One that includes them reads as a project.

docs.title: W9: Last regression run, and what I would hand to the next team
Starting point
docs.text: Everything is written and the demonstration is rehearsed, so this week was the pass that exists to find out whether all of it still runs together after a semester of changes that each worked individually.

docs.title: What I re-ran
docs.text:
• The full user journey, in a browser, against a backup copy of the demonstration database (restored afterwards): borrower login → score and explanation → loan request targeted at a lender → lender approves with a rate → borrower repays an EMI through the demo gateway → score moves → admin sees the loan in the portfolio. Seven steps, four logins, one uninterrupted run.
  • The API error paths that the journey does not exercise: paying another borrower's loan (403), an unknown loan (404), a wallet too small (400 with the shortfall), no token (401), a second decision on an already-decided link (400).
  • The test suite, which comes out at 52 of 54, the two failures being D-01 and D-02 — both known, both written up, neither exposing data.

Nothing new broke. The one surprise was how much the data had moved rather than the code: the loan status breakdown and the default rate are both different from the prototype-stage figures, for reasons that are documented but that I would have been unable to explain from memory a week ago.

docs.title: What I would hand over
docs.text:
If another team picked this up, the four things I would tell them first:

  1. The cold-start blend is the project. Everything else — marketplace, dashboards, anomaly flags — is ordinary CRUD around it. If you change one thing, change that one and measure it.
  2. The demo credentials are not security. Publicly known seeded passwords, a shared hash across borrowers, a hard-coded gateway login, opaque tokens with no rotation. Every one is a deliberate demo shortcut and every one has to go before this touches a real person's data.
  3. The model is trained on 470-odd rows. The monotone constraints make it behave, but no amount of constraint turns that into evidence about real borrowers. Treat the accuracy figures as "the pipeline works", not "the model is good".
  4. Run the migrations and read the README. Both exist because the project was unreproducible for most of its life, and that was the single biggest waste of time in the semester.

docs.title: What I learned that I did not expect to
docs.text:
Most of the real bugs this term were not crashes. The risk labels read backwards, the history chart sloped the wrong way, the score went up after a late payment, a logged-out tab kept showing data, a settled loan still asked for money. Every one of those rendered perfectly, threw no exception, and was wrong.

The habit that caught them was the same each time: read the output and ask whether it could actually be true. Nothing in a test suite does that for you, because a test can only check the thing you already thought to doubt.

docs.title: Week 1 : Session for a Role That Has No Database Row
Error:
docs.text:
Error encountered on the first admin login attempt, POST /api/auth/admin/login.

sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError: (sqlite3.IntegrityError) NOT NULL constraint failed: individual_sessions.individual_id [SQL: INSERT INTO individual_sessions (individual_id, token, created_at, expires_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)][parameters: (None, 'x3d...', '2026-...', '2026-...')]

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
Every other role hangs its session off a business row, so the session table carries a non-null foreign key to it:

class IndividualSession(Base):
    __tablename__ = "individual_sessions"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    individual_id = Column(Integer,
                           ForeignKey("individuals.id"),
                           nullable=False, index=True)
    token = Column(String(64), nullable=False, unique=True,
                   index=True)

I tried to reuse that table for admin by passing None for individual_id, because the bank/analyst who logs in as admin is not a borrower, a lender or an SHG. There is no admin_users table in the schema at all.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text: The failure is not really about a NULL column. It is that I was modelling admin as a business entity when it is actually a credential. Adding an admin_users table would have meant seeding a person who does not exist in the dataset, which our own rule for this project forbids (no fabricated business data).

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Read the credential from configuration, and give admin its own session table with no foreign key at all.

# app/config.py
ADMIN_USERNAME = os.getenv("ADMIN_USERNAME", "admin")
ADMIN_PASSWORD = os.getenv("ADMIN_PASSWORD", "admin123")

# app/models.py
class AdminSession(Base):
    """Admin session -- no FK, since admin is an env-var
    credential, not a business entity (docs/SPEC.md §6)."""
    __tablename__ = "admin_sessions"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    token = Column(String(64), nullable=False, unique=True,
                   index=True)
    created_at = Column(DateTime, default=datetime.utcnow)
    expires_at = Column(DateTime, nullable=False)

The dependency then returns a marker object rather than a row, so nothing downstream can accidentally treat admin as a person:

@dataclass
class AdminActor:
    name: str = "Admin"


def get_current_admin(
    authorization: str | None = Header(default=None),
    db: Session = Depends(get_db),
) -> AdminActor:
    token = _bearer_token(authorization)
    if not auth_service.is_admin_token_valid(db, token):
        raise HTTPException(401, "Not logged in, or your "
                            "session has expired.")
    return AdminActor()

Credential check with a constant-time comparison:

def secrets_compare(a: str, b: str) -> bool:
    import hmac
    return hmac.compare_digest(a, b)

Because

A session table exists to answer "which subject is this token for?". When the subject is a configuration value rather than a stored record, the only honest schema is one that stores the token and nothing else, and the type returned by the dependency should make that emptiness visible to the next reader instead of hiding it behind a fake row.

hmac.compare_digest is used in place of == because a plain string comparison returns early on the first differing character, and that timing difference is measurable. It costs nothing to avoid.

docs.title: Week 2 : Borrower Search Returns 422 and an Empty Table
Client-Side Filtering vs the API Page Cap
Error:
docs.text:
The admin dashboard's borrower browser rendered an empty table with no error message. The network tab showed:

GET /api/individuals?limit=1000 422 (Unprocessable Entity)

{"detail":[{"type":"less_than_equal","loc":["query", "limit"],"msg":"Input should be less than or equal to 500","input":"1000","ctx":{"le":500}}]}

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
My first version of the browser fetched one large page and filtered it in the browser as the admin typed:

// frontend/src/pages/dashboards/AdminDashboard.jsx
const { data } = useApi(() => listIndividuals({ limit: 1000 }))
const rows = (data?.items ?? []).filter(r =>
  r.name.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()))

The endpoint it calls caps the page size:

# app/routers/individuals.py
def list_individuals(
    db: Session = Depends(get_db),
    admin: AdminActor = Depends(get_current_admin),
    search: str | None = None,
    ...
    limit: int = Query(50, le=500),
    offset: int = 0,
):

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
There are two separate faults here, and fixing only the visible one would have been worse than leaving it broken.

  1. limit=1000 violates le=500, so every request fails validation and the table is always empty.
  2. Even with limit=500, the dataset has 1,079 borrowers. Filtering one page in the browser means roughly half the population can never be found by search -- the box would look like it worked while silently lying.

Fault 2 throws no error at all. It only shows up if you search for a borrower you already know exists and notice that they are not returned.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Stop filtering on the client. The endpoint already accepts a search parameter and pushes the work into SQL:

if search:
    term = search.strip()
    like = f"%{term}%"
    conditions = [Individual.name.ilike(like),
                  Individual.phone.ilike(like)]
    if term.isdigit():
        conditions.append(Individual.id == int(term))
    q = q.filter(or_(*conditions))

so the dashboard asks for a small page of matches instead of a large page of everything:

const { data } = useApi(
  () => listIndividuals({ search: debounced, limit: 25 }),
  [debounced])

with a 250 ms debounce on the input so a query is not fired on every keystroke.

Because

A page size that is "big enough" is not a design, it is a guess that expires the moment the data grows. If a list can grow, the filtering has to happen where the data is, and the page size then only decides how much is drawn -- not how much is searchable.

The 422 was the useful part of this bug. The silent half -- a search box that reaches half the population -- is the kind of fault that survives a demo and reaches a user.

docs.title: Week 3 : "High Trust" Printed on the Worst District
k-means Cluster Indices Are Not Ranks
Error:
docs.text:
No exception, no empty response. GET /api/geo/districts returned a district heatmap whose labels were inverted:

[{"name":"...","avg_score":641.2,"default_rate":0.27, "cluster":0,"label":"High Trust"}, {"name":"...","avg_score":752.8,"default_rate":0.11, "cluster":2,"label":"Emerging / Needs Trust-Building"}, ...]

The district labelled High Trust had the lowest average score on the page, and the highest default rate.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The endpoint clusters the ten districts on three standardised features and hands back a label per district:

# app/ml/clustering.py
CLUSTER_LABELS_BY_RANK = ["High Trust", "Moderate",
                          "Emerging / Needs Trust-Building"]

feature_cols = ["avg_score", "default_rate", "shg_density"]
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(df[feature_cols])

km = KMeans(n_clusters=n_clusters, n_init=10,
            random_state=42)
df["cluster"] = km.fit_predict(X)

My first version took the label straight off the cluster index:

df["label"] = df["cluster"].map(
    lambda c: CLUSTER_LABELS_BY_RANK[c])

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
A k-means cluster index carries no meaning whatsoever. It is the order in which the centroids happened to be initialised, nothing more. cluster == 0 is not "the best cluster"; it is "the cluster that was created first".

Mapping an ordered list of labels onto an unordered index produces a result that is confidently, invisibly wrong -- the response is well-formed, every district has a label, and the colours on the heatmap look fine.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Rank the clusters by the quantity the labels are actually about, and map the labels onto that ranking:

# Rank clusters by mean avg_score so labels are meaningful
# ("High Trust" is always the best-scoring cluster), not
# just an arbitrary k-means index.
cluster_rank = (
    df.groupby("cluster")["avg_score"]
      .mean().sort_values(ascending=False).index.tolist()
)
label_for_cluster = {}
for rank, cluster_id in enumerate(cluster_rank):
    if n_clusters == len(CLUSTER_LABELS_BY_RANK):
        label_for_cluster[cluster_id] = \
            CLUSTER_LABELS_BY_RANK[rank]
    else:
        label_for_cluster[cluster_id] = f"Cluster {rank + 1}"

random_state=42 stays fixed as well, so two consecutive page loads over unchanged data cannot return different cluster numbers for the same district.

The regression test asserts the property rather than the numbers, so it does not need updating when the data does:

the district with the highest average score must carry the label "High Trust"

Because

An unsupervised algorithm returns a partition, not an ordering. Any human-readable meaning attached to its output has to be derived from a feature you chose, not from the algorithm's internal bookkeeping.

This is the failure mode I now look for first in anything ML-backed on this dashboard: nothing crashed, nothing was empty, and the meaning was exactly backwards.

docs.title: Week 4 : KeyError on a Field the Artifact Never Had
Error:
docs.text:
Error encountered on GET /api/admin/model-health while building the admin model-health card.

File "app/routers/admin.py", line 61, in model_health "last_computed": meta["trained_at"], ~~~~^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ KeyError: 'trained_at'

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
I wrote the endpoint expecting the scoring artifact to carry a training timestamp and a model version. It does not. The real keys in artifacts/scoring_meta.json are:

>>> json.load(open("artifacts/scoring_meta.json")).keys()
dict_keys(['feature_columns', 'impute_medians',
           'shap_expected_value',
           'trained_on_shg_linked_only',
           'min_repayment_events', 'n_training_rows',
           'holdout_accuracy', 'holdout_auc'])

There is no date and no version anywhere in the file.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
The obvious fix -- add trained_at and version to the artifact -- has two problems. Nothing can be displayed until the model is retrained, and both values would then be numbers we write about ourselves rather than facts about the system.

Both facts already exist elsewhere, as by-products of work that actually happened:

  • when the artifact was last written -> its own modification time on disk;
  • which model produced the newest score in production -> CreditScore.model_version on the most recent row.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
# app/routers/admin.py
meta_path = ARTIFACTS_DIR / "scoring_meta.json"
meta = {}
last_computed = None
if meta_path.exists():
    with open(meta_path) as f:
        meta = json.load(f)
    last_computed = date.fromtimestamp(
        os.path.getmtime(meta_path)).isoformat()

latest_score_row = (
    db.query(CreditScore)
      .order_by(CreditScore.calculated_date.desc()).first()
)
model_version = (latest_score_row.model_version
                 if latest_score_row else None)

Everything else on the card is read from the artifact with .get(), so a missing key renders as blank instead of raising:

"n_training_rows": meta.get("n_training_rows"),
"holdout_accuracy": meta.get("holdout_accuracy"),
"holdout_auc": meta.get("holdout_auc"),

The score distribution needed one more correction. My first query counted every row in credit_scores, which counts a borrower once per rescore. It has to be the latest score per borrower:

select cs.score
from credit_scores cs
join (
    select individual_id, max(calculated_date) as max_date
    from credit_scores group by individual_id
) latest on latest.individual_id = cs.individual_id
        and latest.max_date = cs.calculated_date

Because

meta["k"] asserts that the file has a shape. Reading a file you did not write is exactly the place where that assertion is worth the most and costs the least, so those reads use .get() and the panel degrades to blanks rather than a 500.

The distribution bug is the same mistake in a different place: a plain join over an append-only history table silently answers a question about score rows when the card is asking about people.

docs.title: Also logged this week
docs.text: Testing the admin gate with the other roles' tokens: no token gives 401 everywhere, and a borrower token is refused on every admin-only endpoint, so nothing leaks. But the refusal comes back as 401 from get_current_admin, whereas our specification says a valid token in the wrong role must be 403. Access is still denied; the frontend just cannot tell "logged out" from "not allowed". Raised as defect D-02 rather than patched in a hurry, because the clean fix belongs in the dependency: check whether the token matches any other role's live session, return 403 if it does and 401 only when there is no valid session at all.

docs.title: Week 5 : Re-checking the Admin Gate After the Role Redesign
Error:
docs.text:
After the role-based redesign landed, an admin token on an admin-only endpoint was fine, but a borrower token on the same endpoint came back with the wrong status:

GET /api/individuals Authorization: Bearer

401 {"detail":"Not logged in, or your session has expired -- please log in again."}

Access was refused, which is correct. The status code was not.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
docs/SPEC.md is explicit about the two cases:

  • 401 -- the caller is unknown: no token, an expired token, a token that matches no live session.
  • 403 -- the caller is known, and still not allowed.

The admin dependency makes no such distinction:

def get_current_admin(
    authorization: str | None = Header(default=None),
    db: Session = Depends(get_db),
) -> AdminActor:
    token = _bearer_token(authorization)
    if not auth_service.is_admin_token_valid(db, token):
        raise HTTPException(401, "Not logged in, or your session has "
                            "expired -- please log in again.")
    return AdminActor()

is_admin_token_valid only ever asks "is this an admin session?". A perfectly valid borrower token answers no, exactly as a garbage string does, so both produce 401.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
I walked the whole matrix rather than spot-checking, because a redesign that moves every endpoint behind a dependency is precisely when a gap opens:

Caller Admin-only endpoint Expected Actual no token /api/individuals 401 401 borrower token /api/individuals 403 401 lender token /api/anomalies 403 401 SHG token /api/admin/model-health 403 401 admin token all of the above 200 200 admin token POST /api/links/{id}/decide 403 403

Two things are true at once. Nothing leaks -- every refusal is still a refusal. And the frontend cannot tell the two cases apart, so a logged-in lender who wanders onto an admin URL is bounced to the login page instead of being told they lack access.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Kept as defect D-02 rather than patched in place, because the fix belongs in the dependency and not in the handlers:

# intended shape
def get_current_admin(...):
    token = _bearer_token(authorization)
    if auth_service.is_admin_token_valid(db, token):
        return AdminActor()
    if auth_service.any_role_session_for(db, token):
        raise HTTPException(403, "This area is for the bank/analyst "
                            "login only.")
    raise HTTPException(401, "Not logged in, or your session has expired.")

The admin-only decide endpoint (POST /api/links/{id}/decide) already returns 403 correctly, and stays as the reference behaviour.

Because

A status code is an interface, not decoration. 401 says "tell me who you are" and the only sensible client response is to re-authenticate; 403 says "I know who you are and the answer is still no", where re-authenticating is pointless and the user needs a message. Collapsing the two means the frontend's only possible reaction to either is the wrong one half the time.

Logging it instead of hot-fixing it was deliberate too: the change touches the dependency every admin endpoint shares, and the week's remaining time was better spent proving the gate denies correctly everywhere than rewriting it in a hurry.

docs.title: Week 6 : What an Anomaly Flag Is Allowed To Do
Error:
docs.text:
Not a crash this week. The problem was a design question I had got wrong in my own head, and it showed up as a request during review: "can we subtract points from the flagged borrowers automatically?"

The honest answer is no, and the panel had to be built so that nobody could reasonably assume otherwise.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The detector itself is an Isolation Forest over the behavioural features:

model = IsolationForest(contamination=CONTAMINATION,
                        random_state=42, n_estimators=200)

Each flag carries a plain-language reason rather than only a score:

def _reason_for(row):
    reasons = []
    ...
    reasons.append("unusually large average lateness when late")
    if not reasons:
        reasons.append("behavioural pattern statistically unusual "
                       "relative to peers (see feature values)")
    return "; ".join(reasons)

Rows are listed by anomaly score ascending, because scikit-learn's convention makes the more negative score the more unusual point.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Three properties of the detector decide what the flag may mean:

  1. contamination is an assumption, not a measurement. It fixes the proportion of the population that comes back flagged. Set it to 5% and roughly 5% is flagged -- on clean data as readily as on dirty data. The flag count is therefore not evidence that anything is wrong.
  2. Unusual is not the same as bad. A borrower who repays early every single cycle is as far from the centre of the distribution as one who pays erratically, and the model has no notion of which direction is undesirable.
  3. The model never sees repayment outcomes. It clusters behaviour. Treating its output as a risk verdict would be using a model to answer a question it was not asked.

Put together: a flag is a prompt to look, and nothing more. If it silently moved a score, the system would be penalising people for being statistically unusual, which is not a thing an outlier detector is entitled to do -- and the borrower's SHAP explanation would not even be able to say why their score dropped, because the anomaly flag is not a model feature.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
The panel states its own limits, in the UI copy and in the router docstring, so the constraint survives the next person reading the code:

  • flags are presented as "a prompt for review, not an automatic penalty";
  • no code path from anomaly_flags to credit_scores exists, and the score pipeline does not read the table at all;
  • Re-run detection (POST /api/anomalies/run) recomputes flags from data that already exists -- it creates no business record, which is why it is one of the two compute actions an otherwise read-only admin is allowed;
  • the reason string is shown next to every row, because a bare score tells a reviewer nothing they can act on.

One UI detail cost me time: after clicking Re-run detection the table still showed the previous flags, because the component was not refetching. Added a reload() after the POST resolves, plus a disabled/"Running..." state, since the detector takes a visible moment on the full population and an idle-looking button invites a second click.

Because

The dangerous version of this feature is the one that works. An automatic penalty attached to an unsupervised model is easy to build, looks decisive in a demo, and is wrong in a way nobody notices until a real person is refused a loan for a reason nobody can explain.

Keeping the human in the loop costs one click and leaves the responsibility where it belongs.

docs.title: Week 7 : The Admin Dashboard That Would Not Go Away
Error:
docs.text:
Found while rehearsing the demo. Two tabs open: admin in one, borrower login in the other.

Tab A: logged in as admin, Academic... platform overview on screen. Tab B: log in as a borrower -> borrower dashboard loads. Tab A: still showing the admin dashboard, full of data. Tab A: click anything -> 401, redirected to login.

So the admin view sat there looking live, with platform-wide numbers on screen, after that session had already been replaced.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The frontend keeps one session for the whole browser:

// AuthContext.jsx -- one STORAGE_KEY, shared by every tab
const [auth, setAuth] = useState(() => readStoredAuth())

That is a deliberate decision, not an accident: one role logged in per browser at a time keeps the demo honest and avoids pretending the platform supports a user who is simultaneously a bank and a borrower.

The bug is what happens after the swap. localStorage is shared across tabs, so logging in as the borrower overwrites the stored session -- but React state in tab A was initialised once, at mount, and nothing told it the world had changed. The component tree kept rendering from memory.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
This is only cosmetic until you remember what the admin dashboard displays. Borrower names, scores, district aggregates and anomaly flags stayed on screen for a session that no longer existed. The data was fetched legitimately, before the swap, and no new request would have succeeded -- the server was never confused. But a bystander looking at that tab sees platform-wide data in a window whose owner has logged out, and "it only looks wrong" is not a defence I would want to make about an oversight console.

It also explains a complaint I had dismissed earlier as flakiness: "the dashboard isn't syncing." It was syncing. It had been logged out.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
Raised it with the owner of AuthContext.jsx with the reproduction above, since the session context is shared by all four roles and not mine to rewrite. The fix that went in listens for the storage event, which fires in other tabs when the key changes, and folds the new value straight into auth state:

useEffect(() => {
  // Only one role can be logged in per browser at a time (STORAGE_KEY is
  // shared across tabs by design). Without this, logging into a second
  // role in another tab silently logs out every other tab's session --
  // but their React state keeps showing the stale dashboard until the
  // next navigation/reload, which looks like data "isn't syncing".
  const onStorage = (e) => {
    if (e.key !== STORAGE_KEY) return
    try {
      setAuth(e.newValue ? JSON.parse(e.newValue) : null)
    } catch {
      setAuth(null)
    }
  }
  window.addEventListener('storage', onStorage)
  return () => window.removeEventListener('storage', onStorage)
}, [])

I re-tested the admin side afterwards: tab A drops to the login screen the instant tab B signs in, ProtectedRoute does the rest, and logging out in one tab clears the others the same way. No admin data stays on screen past its session.

Because

Any state copied out of a shared store has to subscribe to that store, or it is a cache with no invalidation. useState(() => read()) reads once; the reader then has no idea the source changed. The storage event exists for exactly this, and it is the browser telling you the assumption you made at mount is no longer true.

The wider lesson for this role: for an oversight dashboard, "the server would have refused the next request" is not sufficient. What is on the screen is part of the access-control surface.

docs.title: Week 8 : Model Health After a Retrain
Error:
docs.text:
The model was retrained during the scoring work, and the health panel started disagreeing with itself:

Model version: v2 (from the newest credit_scores row) Last computed: the artifact's file date -- today Holdout accuracy / AUC: the new artifact's values Borrowers scored: 1,079 / 1,079 Score distribution: unchanged from before the retrain

The distribution could not be right. If every borrower had been rescored by a different model, the bands had to move.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
The panel reads two sources on purpose, because the artifact does not carry everything:

meta_path = ARTIFACTS_DIR / "scoring_meta.json"
if meta_path.exists():
    with open(meta_path) as f:
        meta = json.load(f)
    last_computed = date.fromtimestamp(
        os.path.getmtime(meta_path)).isoformat()

latest_score_row = (
    db.query(CreditScore)
      .order_by(CreditScore.calculated_date.desc()).first()
)
model_version = (latest_score_row.model_version
                 if latest_score_row else None)

last_computed is the artifact's own modification time and model_version comes from the newest score actually stored -- both facts about the system rather than values we write about ourselves.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
The retrain had produced a new artifact. It had not rescored the population. So the panel was telling the truth in a misleading way: the metadata described the model on disk, while the distribution described scores computed by the previous model. Every number was individually correct and the panel as a whole was wrong.

The second finding came from checking the distribution query itself:

select cs.score
from credit_scores cs
join (
    select individual_id, max(calculated_date) as max_date
    from credit_scores group by individual_id
) latest on latest.individual_id = cs.individual_id
        and latest.max_date = cs.calculated_date

That join is load-bearing. credit_scores is append-only, so a plain scan would count a borrower once per rescore -- and a borrower rescored five times would be five rows in the histogram. The panel would then be describing the score history, not the people. With the retrain adding a second row for everyone, this is exactly when the mistake would have started showing.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
• Batch-rescored the population after the retrain, so the stored scores and the stored artifact describe the same model, and the distribution means what the panel says it means.
  • Kept model_version sourced from the newest score row rather than from the artifact, so the panel reports what was actually used in production, not what is sitting on disk waiting to be used. The mismatch above is a condition worth being able to see.
  • Left every artifact read as .get():
"n_training_rows": meta.get("n_training_rows"),
"holdout_accuracy": meta.get("holdout_accuracy"),
"holdout_auc": meta.get("holdout_auc"),

so a key the next retrain does not write renders blank instead of raising a 500 -- the same lesson as the trained_at KeyError in W4.

Because

A dashboard that mixes sources has to be read as a whole, not as a list of independent tiles. Here the tiles came from two different points in time, and nothing on the screen said so.

The underlying rule I keep relearning on this role: when a panel's numbers can disagree, the useful design is the one that lets the disagreement be visible rather than the one that hides it by reading everything from a single convenient place.

docs.title: Week 9 : Verification Pass Before the Final Report
Does the Oversight View Still Add Up?
Error:
docs.text:
Two data migrations and a model retrain landed in the same week, and the admin dashboard sits downstream of all three. The portfolio overview had moved since the figures quoted in the Prototype Stage report:

Prototype Stage report: 1,619 loans, 315 defaulted, default rate 19.4% After the migrations: 1,640 loans, 309 defaulted, default rate 18.8% Active 736 | Closed 595 | Defaulted 309

Nothing was broken. But numbers I had already put in a submitted report had changed, and "the data changed" is not an answer I would want to give in a viva.

docs.title: Relevant Context
docs.text:
Three changes, each from a different part of the system:

migrate_close_paid_loans.py  -- closes Active loans whose
                                outstanding_balance <= 0.01
migrate_loan_lenders.py      -- attributes seeded loans to lenders
train_scoring_model.py       -- retrain with monotone constraints

The seed generator now applies the same close-paid rule when it builds the database, so a regenerated dataset already reflects it. Reseeding and counting shows what the first migration was for:

select status, count(*) from loans group by status;
-- Active 736 | Closed 595 | Defaulted 309

select count(*) from loans
 where status='Closed' and outstanding_balance <= 0.01;
-- 595

select count(*) from loans
 where status='Closed' and outstanding_balance > 0.01;
-- 0

Every single Closed loan is closed because its balance reached zero, not because it reached its final cycle. Under the old rule -- close only on the last cycle and a zero balance -- all 595 of those sat in Active, owing nothing and still payable, because the generator tracks principal-only balances and they hit zero early.

docs.title: Key Observation
docs.text:
Checking invariants is a different exercise from checking numbers, and only the first is repeatable when the data underneath keeps moving:

Invariant Result Active + Closed + Defaulted = total loans 736 + 595 + 309 = 1,640 SHG-linked + independent = total borrowers 659 + 420 = 1,079 default rate = defaulted / total 309 / 1,640 = 18.8% best-scoring district carries the "High Trust" label holds every loan names a lender no -- 74 do not

The last row is the residue of the attribution migration. On the dataset as regenerated today it placed 1,566 seeded loans with a lender and left 74 without one; those render through a fallback rather than a blank cell:

"lender_name": loan.lender.name if loan.lender else "Lender not recorded",

That is correct behaviour, not a defect -- but it is on screen, and I would rather know why before an examiner asks.

The summary endpoint computes the whole breakdown per request instead of storing it:

"n_loans": n_loans, "n_loans_defaulted": n_defaulted,
"n_loans_active": n_active, "n_loans_closed": n_closed,
"default_rate": round(n_defaulted / n_loans, 4) if n_loans else None,

which is why the identity survived a migration that rewrote a third of the rows: there is no cached total to drift out of step.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text:
• Re-ran the test suite: 52 of 54 cases pass, the two failures being the known defects D-01 (all seeded borrowers share one password hash) and D-02 (401 where the specification says 403).
  • Re-checked the admin analytics by hand after the retrain: district clusters still label by rank rather than by k-means index, the identities above hold, the model-health panel reports the retrained artifact against a population rescored by it, and the anomaly list still touches no score.
  • Recorded the before/after portfolio figures and their cause, so the difference between the Prototype Stage report and the Final Report is explainable rather than merely survivable.

Because

A verification pass is not for confirming the screen looks fine. It is for finding the questions an examiner could ask that I could not currently answer -- and the honest finding this week is that a number moving for a good reason looks, from outside, exactly like a number moving because something broke.

Writing the invariants down converts that into a one-minute check every time the data changes, instead of something I have to remember to be suspicious about.

docs.title: What I would do next on this role
docs.text:
• Fix D-02 in get_current_admin; it is small, and it is the only defect on this role's own surface.
  • Give the admin an audit trail before giving it any moderation action. A read-only console that quietly acquires write paths stops being oversight.
  • Cache the score distribution. Recomputing it per request is fine for 1,079 borrowers and stops being fine well before a real population.
